claim: Many environmental stimuli present a quasi-rhythmic structure at different timescales that the brain needs to decompose and integrate.
source: Many environmental stimuli present a quasi-rhythmic structure at different timescales that the brain needs to decompose and integrate.
evidence: This is a general statement about environmental stimuli and brain processing that draws from established understanding in neuroscience.

claim: Cortical oscillations have been proposed as instruments of sensory de-multiplexing, i.e., the parallel processing of different frequency streams in sensory signals.
source: Cortical oscillations have been proposed as instruments of sensory de-multiplexing, i.e., the parallel processing of different frequency streams in sensory signals.
evidence: This statement references a theoretical proposal in the field, implying citation to prior work.

claim: The causal role of cortical oscillations in sensory de-multiplexing has never been demonstrated.
source: Yet their causal role in such a process has never been demonstrated.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the field prior to this work, based on knowledge of existing literature.

claim: In continuous speech, theta oscillations can flexibly track the syllabic rhythm.
source: We show that, in continuous speech, theta oscillations can flexibly track the syllabic rhythm and temporally organize the phoneme-level response of gamma neurons into a code that enables syllable identification.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Theta oscillations temporally organize the phoneme-level response of gamma neurons into a code that enables syllable identification.
source: We show that, in continuous speech, theta oscillations can flexibly track the syllabic rhythm and temporally organize the phoneme-level response of gamma neurons into a code that enables syllable identification.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The tracking of slow speech fluctuations by theta oscillations is a critical feature for accurate speech encoding.
source: The tracking of slow speech fluctuations by theta oscillations, and its coupling to gamma-spiking activity both appeared as critical features for accurate speech encoding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the full model with control models in the simulations.

claim: The coupling of theta oscillations to gamma-spiking activity is a critical feature for accurate speech encoding.
source: The tracking of slow speech fluctuations by theta oscillations, and its coupling to gamma-spiking activity both appeared as critical features for accurate speech encoding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the full model with control models in the simulations.

claim: Cortical oscillations can be a key instrument of speech de-multiplexing, parsing, and encoding.
source: These results demonstrate that cortical oscillations can be a key instrument of speech de-multiplexing, parsing, and encoding.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the modeling results.

claim: Speech contains different rhythms that index linguistic representations of different granularities, from phoneme to syllables and words.
source: Speech constitutes an example of such a physical complexity, in which different rhythms index linguistic representations of different granularities, from phoneme to syllables and words (Rosen, 1992; Zion Golumbic et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Before meaning can be extracted from continuous speech, a de-multiplexing step (parallel analysis of each constitutive rhythm) needs to be carried out.
source: Before meaning can be extracted from continuous speech, two critical pre-processing steps need to be carried out: a de-multiplexing step, i.e., the parallel analysis of each constitutive rhythm, and a parsing step, i.e., the discretization of the acoustic signal into linguistically relevant chunks that can be individually processed (Stevens, 2002; Poeppel, 2003; Ghitza, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Before meaning can be extracted from continuous speech, a parsing step (discretization of the acoustic signal into linguistically relevant chunks) needs to be carried out.
source: Before meaning can be extracted from continuous speech, two critical pre-processing steps need to be carried out: a de-multiplexing step, i.e., the parallel analysis of each constitutive rhythm, and a parsing step, i.e., the discretization of the acoustic signal into linguistically relevant chunks that can be individually processed (Stevens, 2002; Poeppel, 2003; Ghitza, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Parsing is presumably modulated in a top-down way by knowing a priori through developmental learning where linguistic boundaries should lie.
source: While parsing is presumably modulated in a top-down way, by knowing a priori through developmental learning (Ngon et al., 2013) where linguistic boundaries should lie, it is likely largely guided by speech acoustic dynamics.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by a citation.

claim: Parsing is likely largely guided by speech acoustic dynamics.
source: While parsing is presumably modulated in a top-down way, by knowing a priori through developmental learning (Ngon et al., 2013) where linguistic boundaries should lie, it is likely largely guided by speech acoustic dynamics.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim that involves speculation about the mechanisms of parsing.

claim: Speech de-multiplexing and parsing could both be handled in a bottom-up way by the combined action of auditory cortical oscillations in distinct frequency ranges.
source: It has recently been proposed that speech de-multiplexing and parsing could both be handled in a bottom-up way by the combined action of auditory cortical oscillations in distinct frequency ranges, enabling parallel computations at syllabic and phonemic timescales (Ghitza, 2011; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Intrinsic coupling across cortical oscillations of distinct frequencies is observed in electrophysiological recordings of auditory cortex.
source: Intrinsic coupling across cortical oscillations of distinct frequencies, as observed in electrophysiological recordings of auditory cortex (Lakatos et al., 2005; Fontolan et al., 2014), could enable the hierarchical combination of syllabic- and phonemic-scale computations, subsequently restoring the natural arrangement of phonemes within syllables (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: This is an empirical observation supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Cross-frequency coupling could enable the hierarchical combination of syllabic- and phonemic-scale computations.
source: Intrinsic coupling across cortical oscillations of distinct frequencies, as observed in electrophysiological recordings of auditory cortex (Lakatos et al., 2005; Fontolan et al., 2014), could enable the hierarchical combination of syllabic- and phonemic-scale computations, subsequently restoring the natural arrangement of phonemes within syllables (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: The most pronounced energy fluctuations in speech occur at about 4 Hz.
source: The most pronounced energy fluctuations in speech occur at about 4 Hz (Zion Golumbic et al., 2012) and can serve as an acoustic guide for signalling the syllabic rhythm (Mermelstein, 1975).
evidence: This is an empirical observation supported by a citation.

claim: Energy fluctuations at about 4 Hz can serve as an acoustic guide for signalling the syllabic rhythm.
source: The most pronounced energy fluctuations in speech occur at about 4 Hz (Zion Golumbic et al., 2012) and can serve as an acoustic guide for signalling the syllabic rhythm (Mermelstein, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The syllabic rate coincides with the auditory cortex theta rhythm (3–8 Hz).
source: Since the syllabic rate coincides with the auditory cortex theta rhythm (3–8 Hz), syllable boundaries could be viably signalled by a given phase in the theta cycle.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about speech rates and neural oscillations.

claim: Syllable boundaries could be viably signalled by a given phase in the theta cycle.
source: Since the syllabic rate coincides with the auditory cortex theta rhythm (3–8 Hz), syllable boundaries could be viably signalled by a given phase in the theta cycle.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference based on the correspondence between syllabic rate and theta frequency.

claim: Speech intelligibility depends on the degree of phase-locking of the theta-range neural activity in auditory cortex.
source: The relevance of speech tracking by the theta neural rhythm (Henry et al., 2014) is highlighted by experimental data showing that speech intelligibility depends on the degree of phase-locking of the theta-range neural activity in auditory cortex (Ahissar et al., 2001; Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Peelle et al., 2013; Gross et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an empirical finding supported by multiple citations.

claim: The theta oscillation may orchestrate gamma neural activity to facilitate its subsequent decoding.
source: By analogy with the spatial and mnemonic oscillatory processes that take place in the hippocampus (Jensen and Lisman, 1996; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Lever et al., 2014), the theta oscillation may orchestrate gamma neural activity to facilitate its subsequent decoding (Canolty et al., 2007): the phase of theta-paced neural activity could regulate faster neural activity in the low-gamma range (>30 Hz) involved in linguistic coding of phonemic details (Ghitza, 2011; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on analogy with hippocampal processes and supported by citations.

claim: The phase of theta-paced neural activity could regulate faster neural activity in the low-gamma range (>30 Hz) involved in linguistic coding of phonemic details.
source: By analogy with the spatial and mnemonic oscillatory processes that take place in the hippocampus (Jensen and Lisman, 1996; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Lever et al., 2014), the theta oscillation may orchestrate gamma neural activity to facilitate its subsequent decoding (Canolty et al., 2007): the phase of theta-paced neural activity could regulate faster neural activity in the low-gamma range (>30 Hz) involved in linguistic coding of phonemic details (Ghitza, 2011; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: The control of gamma by theta oscillations could modulate the excitability of gamma neurons to devote more processing power to the informative parts of syllabic sound patterns.
source: The control of gamma by theta oscillations could hence both modulate the excitability of gamma neurons to devote more processing power to the informative parts of syllabic sound patterns, and constitute a reference time frame aligned on syllabic contours for interpreting gamma-based phonemic processing (Shamir et al., 2009; Ghitza, 2011; Kayser et al., 2012; Panzeri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: The control of gamma by theta oscillations could constitute a reference time frame aligned on syllabic contours for interpreting gamma-based phonemic processing.
source: The control of gamma by theta oscillations could hence both modulate the excitability of gamma neurons to devote more processing power to the informative parts of syllabic sound patterns, and constitute a reference time frame aligned on syllabic contours for interpreting gamma-based phonemic processing (Shamir et al., 2009; Ghitza, 2011; Kayser et al., 2012; Panzeri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Direct evidence for neural mechanisms linking speech constituents and oscillatory components is still lacking.
source: Compelling as this hypothesis may sound, direct evidence for neural mechanisms linking speech constituents and oscillatory components is still lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on knowledge of existing literature.

claim: Previous models of speech processing involved only gamma oscillations in the context of isolated speech segments.
source: Previous models of speech processing involved only gamma oscillations in the context of isolated speech segments (Shamir et al., 2009) or did not involve neural oscillations at all (Gütig and Sompolinsky, 2009; Yildiz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work supported by citations.

claim: Previous models of cross-frequency coupled oscillations did not address sensory functions as parsing and de-multiplexing.
source: On the other hand, previous models of cross-frequency coupled oscillations did not address sensory functions as parsing and de-multiplexing (Jensen and Lisman, 1996; Tort et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work supported by citations.

claim: The model is inspired from cortical architecture and function.
source: The model proposed here (Figure 1A) is inspired from cortical architecture (Douglas and Martin, 2004; da Costa and Martin, 2010) and function (Lakatos et al., 2007) as well as from previous biophysical models of cross-frequency coupled oscillation generation (Tort et al., 2007; Kopell et al., 2010; Vierling-Claassen et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the basis of the model design, supported by citations.

claim: The model uses the Pyramidal Interneuron Gamma (PING) model for implementing a gamma network.
source: We used the well documented Pyramidal Interneuron Gamma (PING) model for implementing a gamma network: bursts of inhibitory neurons immediately follow bursts of excitatory neurons (Jadi and Sejnowski, 2014), creating the overall spiking rhythm.
evidence: This describes a component of the model architecture, supported by a citation.

claim: Gamma and theta oscillations are both locally present in superficial cortical layers.
source: Given that gamma and theta oscillations are both locally present in superficial cortical layers (Lakatos et al., 2005), we assume similar local generation mechanisms for theta and gamma with a direct connection between them.
evidence: This is an empirical observation supported by a citation.

claim: Neocortical (somatosensory) theta oscillations are observed in vitro.
source: Yet, we built the case for local generation from the following facts: (1) neocortical (somatosensory) theta oscillations are observed in vitro (Fanselow et al., 2008), (2) MEG, EEG, and combined EEG/FMRI recordings in humans show that theta activity phase-locks to speech amplitude envelope in A1 and immediate association cortex—but not beyond—(Ahissar et al., 2001; Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Cogan and Poeppel, 2011; Morillon et al., 2012), and (3) theta phase-locking to speech is not accompanied by power increase, arguing for a phase restructuring of a local oscillation (Luo and Poeppel, 2007).
evidence: This is an empirical observation supported by a citation.

claim: Theta activity phase-locks to speech amplitude envelope in A1 and immediate association cortex but not beyond.
source: Yet, we built the case for local generation from the following facts: (1) neocortical (somatosensory) theta oscillations are observed in vitro (Fanselow et al., 2008), (2) MEG, EEG, and combined EEG/FMRI recordings in humans show that theta activity phase-locks to speech amplitude envelope in A1 and immediate association cortex—but not beyond—(Ahissar et al., 2001; Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Cogan and Poeppel, 2011; Morillon et al., 2012), and (3) theta phase-locking to speech is not accompanied by power increase, arguing for a phase restructuring of a local oscillation (Luo and Poeppel, 2007).
evidence: This is an empirical observation supported by multiple citations.

claim: Theta phase-locking to speech is not accompanied by power increase, arguing for a phase restructuring of a local oscillation.
source: Yet, we built the case for local generation from the following facts: (1) neocortical (somatosensory) theta oscillations are observed in vitro (Fanselow et al., 2008), (2) MEG, EEG, and combined EEG/FMRI recordings in humans show that theta activity phase-locks to speech amplitude envelope in A1 and immediate association cortex—but not beyond—(Ahissar et al., 2001; Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Cogan and Poeppel, 2011; Morillon et al., 2012), and (3) theta phase-locking to speech is not accompanied by power increase, arguing for a phase restructuring of a local oscillation (Luo and Poeppel, 2007).
evidence: This is an empirical observation and inference supported by a citation.

claim: The model assumes a similar generation mechanism for theta and gamma oscillations, with slower excitatory and inhibitory synaptic time constants for theta.
source: We assumed a similar generation mechanism for theta and gamma oscillations, with slower excitatory and inhibitory synaptic time constants for theta (Kopell et al., 2010; Vierling-Claassen et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes a design choice in the model, supported by citations.

claim: The distinct dynamics for the two modules reflect the diversity of inhibitory synaptic timescales observed experimentally, with Martinotti cells displaying slow synaptic inhibition and basket cells showing faster inhibition decay.
source: The distinct dynamics for the two modules reflect the diversity of inhibitory synaptic timescales observed experimentally, with Martinotti cells displaying slow synaptic inhibition (Ti neurons), and basket cells showing faster inhibition decay (Gi neurons) (Silberberg and Markram, 2007).
evidence: This is an empirical observation supported by a citation.

claim: The full model is composed of a theta-generating module with interconnected spiking excitatory (Te) and inhibitory (Ti) neurons that spontaneously synchronize at theta frequency (6–8 Hz) through slow decaying inhibition.
source: The full model is hence composed of a theta-generating module with interconnected spiking excitatory (Te) and inhibitory (Ti) neurons that spontaneously synchronize at theta frequency (6–8 Hz) through slow decaying inhibition; and of a gamma-generating module with excitatory (Ge) and inhibitory (Gi) neurons that burst at a faster rate (25–45 Hz) synchronized by fast decaying inhibition (PING; Figure 1B) (Börgers and Kopell, 2005).
evidence: This describes the model architecture, supported by a citation.

claim: The full model includes a gamma-generating module with excitatory (Ge) and inhibitory (Gi) neurons that burst at a faster rate (25–45 Hz) synchronized by fast decaying inhibition.
source: The full model is hence composed of a theta-generating module with interconnected spiking excitatory (Te) and inhibitory (Ti) neurons that spontaneously synchronize at theta frequency (6–8 Hz) through slow decaying inhibition; and of a gamma-generating module with excitatory (Ge) and inhibitory (Gi) neurons that burst at a faster rate (25–45 Hz) synchronized by fast decaying inhibition (PING; Figure 1B) (Börgers and Kopell, 2005).
evidence: This describes the model architecture, supported by a citation.

claim: The firing pattern of simulated neurons is sparse and weakly synchronous at rest, consistent with the low spiking rate of cortical neurons.
source: The firing pattern of our simulated neurons is sparse and weakly synchronous at rest, consistent with the low spiking rate of cortical neurons (Brunel and Wang, 2003) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a property of the model that is consistent with empirical observations, supported by a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: The network produced a lower gamma frequency around 30 Hz, as observed in human auditory cortex in response to speech.
source: Unlike the classical 50–80 Hz PING seen in in vitro preparations of rat auditory cortex (Ainsworth et al., 2011), our network produced a lower gamma frequency around 30 Hz, as observed in human auditory cortex in response to speech (Nourski et al., 2009; Pasley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a property of the model that matches empirical observations, supported by citations.

claim: The neural network produced activity in theta (6–8 Hz) and low gamma (25–45 Hz) ranges, both at rest and during speech presentation.
source: As expected from its architecture and biophysical parameters (see 'Materials and methods'), the neural network produced activity in theta (6–8 Hz) and low gamma (25–45 Hz) ranges, both at rest and during speech presentation.
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations.

claim: There was no notable increase in theta spiking during speech presentation.
source: Consistent with experimental observations (Luo and Poeppel, 2007) there was no notable increase in theta spiking during speech presentation, but sentence onsets induced a phase-locking of theta oscillations as shown by the Post-stimulus time histograms of theta neurons, which was further enhanced by all edges in speech envelope.
evidence: This is a result from the model that is consistent with experimental observations, supported by a citation.

claim: Sentence onsets induced a phase-locking of theta oscillations.
source: Consistent with experimental observations (Luo and Poeppel, 2007) there was no notable increase in theta spiking during speech presentation, but sentence onsets induced a phase-locking of theta oscillations as shown by the Post-stimulus time histograms of theta neurons, which was further enhanced by all edges in speech envelope.
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations.

claim: The resulting global evoked activity followed the acoustic envelope of the speech signal.
source: Consequently, the resulting global evoked activity followed the acoustic envelope of the speech signal (Figure 1C) (Abrams et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a result from the model, supported by a figure reference and citation.

claim: The LFP theta phase pattern was robust across repetitions of the same sentence.
source: Unlike the LFP theta power pattern, the LFP theta phase pattern was robust across repetitions of the same sentence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C,E), replicating LFP behaviour from the primate auditory cortex (Kayser et al., 2009), and human MEG data (Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Luo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a result from the model that replicates empirical observations, supported by figure references and citations.

claim: Gamma oscillations followed the onset of sentences.
source: In line with other empirical data from human auditory cortex (Nourski et al., 2009) gamma oscillations followed the onset of sentences (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the model that is consistent with empirical data, supported by a citation and figure reference.

claim: The gamma amplitude was coupled to the theta phase both at rest and during speech.
source: Owing to the feed-forward connection from the theta to the gamma sub-circuits, the gamma amplitude was coupled to the theta phase both at rest and during speech (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations, shown in a figure.

claim: The theta-gamma coupling disappeared when the theta/gamma connection was removed.
source: Critically, this coupling disappeared when the theta/gamma connection was removed, showing that a common input to Te and Ge cells is not sufficient to couple the two oscillations.
evidence: This is a result from control simulations demonstrating the importance of the theta-gamma connection.

claim: A common input to Te and Ge cells is not sufficient to couple the two oscillations.
source: Critically, this coupling disappeared when the theta/gamma connection was removed, showing that a common input to Te and Ge cells is not sufficient to couple the two oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control simulation results.

claim: The acoustic analysis of TIMIT sentences confirmed a correspondence between the dominant peak of the speech modulation spectrum and the mean syllabic rate (3–6 Hz).
source: The acoustic analysis of these sentences confirmed a correspondence between the dominant peak of the speech modulation spectrum and the mean syllabic rate (3–6 Hz) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), whereby syllabic boundaries correspond to trough in speech slow fluctuations (Peelle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an analysis result from the TIMIT corpus, supported by a figure reference and citation.

claim: Syllabic boundaries correspond to trough in speech slow fluctuations.
source: The acoustic analysis of these sentences confirmed a correspondence between the dominant peak of the speech modulation spectrum and the mean syllabic rate (3–6 Hz) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), whereby syllabic boundaries correspond to trough in speech slow fluctuations (Peelle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and figure reference.

claim: When presenting sentences to the theta module, there was a consistent theta burst within 50 ms following syllable onset.
source: When presenting sentences to the theta module, we observed a consistent theta burst within 50 ms following syllable onset followed by a locking of theta oscillations to theta acoustic fluctuations in the speech signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations, shown in a figure.

claim: Neuronal theta bursts closely aligned to the timing of syllable boundaries in the presented sentences.
source: More importantly, neuronal theta bursts closely aligned to the timing of syllable boundaries in the presented sentences (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations, shown in a figure.

claim: The theta network performed better than both the linear model and the Mermelstein algorithm in syllable boundary detection.
source: The theta network performed better than both the linear model and the Mermelstein algorithm (Figure 2B, all p-values <10−12).
evidence: This is a comparison result from the model evaluation, shown in a figure with statistical support.

claim: The theta network could adapt to different speech rates.
source: Similar to results from behavioural studies of human perception (Miller et al., 1984; Nourski et al., 2009; Mukamel et al., 2011) the theta network could adapt to different speech rates.
evidence: This is a result from the model that is similar to behavioral observations, supported by citations.

claim: The model performed better than other algorithms, with syllabic alignment accuracy remaining well above chance levels in the twofold and threefold time compression conditions.
source: The model performed better than other algorithms, with a syllabic alignment accuracy remaining well above chance levels (p < 10−12) in the twofold and threefold time compression conditions. (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the model evaluation with statistical support, shown in a figure.

claim: Using spike patterns, syllable decoding reached a high level of accuracy in the intact model: 58% of syllables were correctly classified within a set of 10 possible syllables.
source: When using spike patterns syllable decoding reached a high level of accuracy in the intact model: 58% of syllables were correctly classified within a set of 10 possible (randomly chosen) syllables (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from the model decoding analysis, shown in a figure.

claim: Syllable decoding dropped when using spike counts instead of spike patterns.
source: Syllable decoding dropped when using spike counts instead of spike patterns (p < 10−12).
evidence: This is a comparison result from the model with statistical support.

claim: Decoding was poor in both control models (undriven theta and uncoupled theta/gamma) using either spike counts or spike patterns.
source: Critically, decoding was poor in both control models (undriven theta and uncoupled theta/gamma) using either spike counts or spike patterns (significantly lower than decoding using spike patterns in the full model, all p-values < 10−12, and non-significantly higher than decoding using spike counts in the full model, all p-values > 0.08 uncorrected).
evidence: This is a result from control model comparisons with statistical support.

claim: When decoding from spike pattern, the intact model allowed 24% accuracy (chance level at 10%) across speakers.
source: When decoding from spike pattern, the intact model allowed 24% accuracy (chance level at 10%).
evidence: This is a result from the cross-speaker decoding analysis.

claim: The intact model showed a peak in performance for syllables durations between 100 and 300 ms.
source: Accordingly, decoding accuracy was not uniform across the whole syllable duration range. When decoding from spike pattern, the intact model allowed 24% accuracy (chance level at 10%). It showed a peak in performance in the range in which it is expected to operate, i.e., for syllables durations between 100 and 300 ms.
evidence: This is a result from the syllable duration analysis.

claim: The intact model outperformed control models both within the 100 to 300 ms range and throughout the whole syllable duration span.
source: Critically, the intact model outperformed control models both within the 100 to 300 ms range (p < 0.001), and throughout the whole syllable duration span (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a comparison result with statistical support.

claim: While degrading, the decoding performance remained above chance for compression rates of 2 and 3, mimicking humans decoding performance.
source: Lastly, we tested more directly the resilience of the spike pattern code to speech temporal compression and found that while degrading the decoding performance remained above chance for compression rates of 2 and 3 (Figure 4D), mimicking humans decoding performance (Ahissar et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a result from the compression analysis that mimics human performance, supported by a citation and figure reference.

claim: For 80 to 240 ms windows (within one theta cycle), decoding was almost as good for the phase-partitioned code as for the time-partitioned code.
source: We observed that for 80 to 240 ms windows (within one theta cycle), decoding was almost as good for the phase-partitioned code as for the time-partitioned code (Figure 5B, left).
evidence: This is a result from the classification analysis, shown in a figure.

claim: Stimulus decoding using theta timing was nearly as good as when using stimulus timing.
source: In other words, stimulus decoding using theta timing was nearly as good as when using stimulus timing.
evidence: This is an inference from the classification results.

claim: Performance using the spike count was considerably lower than time-partitioned or phase-partitioned codes.
source: Performance using the spike count was considerably lower (p < 10−12 for all 6 window sizes).
evidence: This is a comparison result with statistical support.

claim: There was a qualitative and even quantitative match between the results from simulated data and the original experimental results.
source: Overall, there was a qualitative and even quantitative match between the results from simulated data and the original experimental results (Figure 5B, right).
evidence: This is a comparison between model results and experimental data, shown in a figure.

claim: When the input-to-theta or the theta-to-gamma connection was removed in the network, the performance of the phase-partitioned code dropped to just above that of the spike count code.
source: When we removed either the input-to-theta (undriven theta model) or the theta-to-gamma connection (uncoupled theta/gamma model) in the network, the performance of the phase-partitioned code dropped to just above that of the spike count code (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; significantly lower increase in decoding performance using phase-partitioned instead of spike count code compared to full model, p < 10−12 for all 6 window sizes and both control models), and the simulations no longer predicted the experimental results.
evidence: This is a result from control model comparisons with statistical support, shown in a figure.

claim: Taking into account the spike phase boosts the MI carried by the Spike count code or the Time-partitioned code alone.
source: Figure 5C shows that taking into account the spike phase boosts the MI carried by the Spike count code or the Time-partitioned code alone (p < 10−12 for all 6 window sizes).
evidence: This is a result from the mutual information analysis with statistical support, shown in a figure.

claim: Spike phase provided additional rather than redundant information to more traditional codes.
source: In other words, spike phase provided additional rather than redundant information to more traditional codes.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutual information results.

claim: The gain provided by spike phase increased when enlarging the window and when combined with either spike count or spike pattern.
source: The gain provided by spike phase increased when enlarging the window and when combined with either spike count or spike pattern (Spike Count vs Time-partitioned; Spike count and Phase-partitioned code vs Time- and Phase-partitioned code).
evidence: This is a result from the mutual information analysis.

claim: The mutual information results replicate the original experimental data from monkey auditory cortex.
source: These results replicate the original experimental data from monkey auditory cortex (Kayser et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to experimental data, supported by a citation.

claim: The pattern of mutual information results was not reproduced using any of the control models.
source: Such a pattern was not reproduced using any of the control models (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a result from control model comparisons, shown in a figure.

claim: The theta–gamma connection enhanced the reliability of the spike phase code.
source: These results hence show that in addition to enhancing the reliability of the spike phase code, the theta–gamma connection enhanced the temporal precision of Ge neurons spiking in response to speech stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference from the encoding analysis results.

claim: The theta–gamma connection enhanced the temporal precision of Ge neurons spiking in response to speech stimuli.
source: These results hence show that in addition to enhancing the reliability of the spike phase code, the theta–gamma connection enhanced the temporal precision of Ge neurons spiking in response to speech stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference from the encoding analysis results.

claim: The full network architecture of the model provides an efficient way of boosting the encoding capacity of neurons in a way that bears remarkable similarities to actual neurons from primate auditory cortex.
source: Critically, results from both classifier and mutual information analyses demonstrate that the full network architecture of the model provides an efficient way of boosting the encoding capacity of neurons in a way that bears remarkable similarities to actual neurons from primate auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the encoding analyses comparing model to experimental data.

claim: Theta bursts generated by a theta (PINTH) network can predict 'on-line' syllable boundaries at least as accurately as state-of-the-art offline syllable detection algorithms.
source: The current modelling data demonstrate that theta bursts generated by a theta (PINTH) network can predict 'on-line' syllable boundaries at least as accurately as state-of-the-art offline syllable detection algorithms.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the syllable boundary detection analysis.

claim: Syllable boundary detection by a theta network provides an endogenous time reference for speech decoding.
source: Syllable boundary detection by a theta network hence provides an endogenous time reference for speech decoding.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: A gamma biophysical network, receiving a spectral decomposition of speech as input, can take advantage of the theta time reference to encode fast phonemic information.
source: Our simulated data further show that a gamma biophysical network, receiving a spectral decomposition of speech as input, can take advantage of the theta time reference to encode fast phonemic information.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the decoding analyses.

claim: The gamma network could efficiently encode temporal patterns (from simple sawtooths to natural speech), as long as it was entrained by the theta rhythm driven by syllable boundaries.
source: The central result of our work is that the gamma network could efficiently encode temporal patterns (from simple sawtooths to natural speech), as long as it was entrained by the theta rhythm driven by syllable boundaries.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the encoding analyses.

claim: The proposed theta/gamma network displayed sophisticated spectral and encoding properties that compared both qualitatively and quantitatively to existing neurophysiological evidence including cross-frequency coupling properties.
source: The proposed theta/gamma network displayed sophisticated spectral and encoding properties that compared both qualitatively and quantitatively to existing neurophysiological evidence including cross-frequency coupling properties (Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009) and theta-referenced stimulus encoding (Kayser et al., 2009; 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of the model validation against experimental data, supported by citations.

claim: The projections from the Te to Ge neurons endowed the network with phase-amplitude and phase-frequency coupling between gamma and theta oscillations, at both the spike and the LFP levels.
source: The projections from the Te to Ge neurons endowed the network with phase-amplitude and phase-frequency coupling between gamma and theta oscillations, at both the spike and the LFP levels (Jensen and Colgin, 2007).
evidence: This is a result from the model analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: The model closely reproduces the theta/gamma phase-amplitude coupling observed from intracortical recordings.
source: This closely reproduces the theta/gamma phase-amplitude coupling observed from intracortical recordings (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Lakatos et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a comparison to experimental observations, supported by citations.

claim: Due to the dissociation of excitatory populations, the model obtained denser gamma spiking immediately after the theta burst evoked by the syllable onset.
source: Importantly, due to the dissociation of excitatory populations we obtained denser gamma spiking immediately after the theta burst evoked by the syllable onset.
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations.

claim: A more in-depth encoding is carried-out by the auditory cortex during the early phase of syllables, when more information needs to be extracted.
source: This validates a critical point of theta/gamma parsing system, namely that a more in-depth encoding is carried-out by the auditory cortex during the early phase of syllables, when more information needs to be extracted (Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical point validated by the model results, supported by citations.

claim: Speech can double in speed from one speaker to another and yet remain intelligible up to an artificial compression factor of 3.
source: Speech can double in speed from one speaker to another and yet remain intelligible up to an artificial compression factor of 3 (Ahissar et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an empirical observation about human speech perception, supported by a citation.

claim: In the current model, theta bursts could still signal syllable boundaries when speech was compressed by a factor 2.
source: In the current model, theta bursts could still signal syllable boundaries when speech was compressed by a factor 2 and this alignment deteriorated for higher compression factors.
evidence: This is a result from the compression analysis.

claim: Syllable decoding was significantly degraded for compressed speech, yet remained twice as accurate as chance.
source: Syllable decoding was significantly degraded for compressed speech, yet remained twice as accurate as chance.
evidence: This is a result from the compression analysis.

claim: High level linguistic processes and representations play an important role in speech perception.
source: Our network is purely bottom-up and does not include high level linguistic processes and representations, which in all likelihood plays an important role in speech perception (Davis et al., 2011; Peelle et al., 2013; Gagnepain et al., 2012): its relative resilience to speech compression is thus a fairly good performance.
evidence: This is a statement about speech perception supported by citations.

claim: A previous model proposed a neural code that was robust to speech warping, based on the notion that individual neurons correct for speech rate by their overall level of activity.
source: A previous model (Gütig and Sompolinsky, 2009) proposed a neural code that was robust to speech warping, based on the notion that individual neurons correct for speech rate by their overall level of activity.
evidence: This is a description of prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: The Gütig and Sompolinsky model achieved very good speech categorization performance but relied on extremely precise spiking behaviour for which neurophysiological evidence is scarce.
source: While this model achieved very good speech categorization performance, it relied on extremely precise spiking behaviour (neurons spiked only once, when their associated channel reached a certain threshold), for which neurophysiological evidence is scarce.
evidence: This is a critique of prior work based on knowledge of neurophysiology.

claim: Hopfield's model proposes that a low gamma external current provides encoding neurons with reliable timing and dynamical memory spanning up to 200 ms.
source: Another model developed by Hopfield proposes that a low gamma external current provides encoding neurons with reliable timing and dynamical memory spanning up to 200 ms, a long enough window to integrate information over a full syllable (Hopfield, 2004).
evidence: This is a description of prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: The advantage of the current model is that integration over long speech segments is permanently enabled by the phase of output spikes with respect to the ongoing theta oscillation.
source: The advantage of our model is that integration over long speech segments is permanently enabled by the phase of output spikes with respect to the ongoing theta oscillation.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantage of the current model based on its design.

claim: Accurate encoding can be achieved using a system that does not require explicit memory processes, and in which the temporal integration buffer is only emulated by a slow neural oscillator aligned to speech dynamics.
source: Our approach shows that accurate encoding can be achieved using a system that does not require explicit memory processes, and in which the temporal integration buffer is only emulated by a slow neural oscillator aligned to speech dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the model's approach based on the results.

claim: Theta oscillations act as a precise neural timer.
source: In the current combined theta/gamma model, theta oscillations do not only act as a syllable-scale integration buffer, but also as a precise neural timer.
evidence: This is a characterization of the model's mechanism.

claim: The theta oscillator can flexibly entrain to syllabic contours (3–7 Hz) and signal syllable boundaries.
source: Because syllabic contours are reflected in the slow modulations of speech, the theta oscillator can flexibly entrain to them (3–7 Hz, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and signal syllable boundaries.
evidence: This is a result from the model analysis, shown in a figure.

claim: The spiking behaviour of theta neurons parallels experimental observations that a subset of neurons in A1 respond to the onset of naturalistic sounds.
source: The spiking behaviour of theta neurons parallels experimental observations that a subset of neurons in A1 respond to the onset of naturalistic sounds (Fishbach et al., 2001; Phillips et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2008), providing an endogenous time reference that serves as a landmark to decode from other neurons (Kayser et al., 2012; Brasselet et al., 2012; Panzeri and Diamond, 2010; Panzeri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to experimental observations, supported by citations.

claim: Theta neurons provide an endogenous time reference that serves as a landmark to decode from other neurons.
source: The spiking behaviour of theta neurons parallels experimental observations that a subset of neurons in A1 respond to the onset of naturalistic sounds (Fishbach et al., 2001; Phillips et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2008), providing an endogenous time reference that serves as a landmark to decode from other neurons (Kayser et al., 2012; Brasselet et al., 2012; Panzeri and Diamond, 2010; Panzeri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a functional interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Theta neurons did not only discharge at stimulus onset but at regular landmarks along the speech signal, the syllable boundaries.
source: In the model, however, theta neurons did not only discharge at stimulus onset but at regular landmarks along the speech signal, the syllable boundaries (Zhou and Wang, 2010).
evidence: This is a result from the model, supported by a citation.

claim: Theta neurons tie together the fast neural activity of gamma excitatory neurons into strings of linguistically relevant chunks (syllables), acting like punctuation in written language.
source: These neurons, hence, tie together the fast neural activity of gamma excitatory neurons into strings of linguistically relevant chunks (syllables), acting like punctuation in written language (Lisman and Buzsáki, 2008).
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the model mechanism, supported by a citation.

claim: The mechanism for segmentation is conceptually similar to the segmentation of neural codes by theta oscillations in the hippocampus during spatial navigation.
source: This mechanism for segmentation is conceptually similar to the segmentation of neural codes by theta oscillations in the hippocampus during spatial navigation (Gupta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison to another neural system, supported by a citation.

claim: The theta rhythm might have been incorporated as a speech-parsing tool in the course of language evolution.
source: From an evolutionary viewpoint, because the theta rhythm is neither auditory- nor human-specific, it might have been incorporated as a speech-parsing tool in the course of language evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary claim.

claim: Human language presumably optimized the length of its main constituents, syllables, to the parsing capacity of the auditory cortex.
source: Likewise, human language presumably optimized the length of its main constituents, syllables, to the parsing capacity of the auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary claim.

claim: Syllables have the ideal temporal format to interface with hippocampal memory processes or with motor routines reflecting other types of rhythmic mechanical constrains.
source: As a result, syllables have the ideal temporal format to interface with, e.g., hippocampal memory processes, or with motor routines reflecting other types of rhythmic mechanical constrains, e.g., the natural motion rate of the jaw (4Hz) (Lieberman, 1985).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about syllable function, supported by a citation.

claim: The current model is purely bottom-up.
source: Although conceptually promising, syllable tracking and speech encoding by a theta/gamma network, as proposed here, also show some limitations. While our current model is purely bottom-up, top-down predictions play a significant role in guiding speech perception (Arnal and Giraud, 2012; Gagnepain et al., 2012; Poeppel et al., 2008) presumably across different frequency channels and processing timescales (Wang, 2010; Bastos et al., 2012; Fontolan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the model.

claim: Top-down predictions play a significant role in guiding speech perception.
source: Although conceptually promising, syllable tracking and speech encoding by a theta/gamma network, as proposed here, also show some limitations. While our current model is purely bottom-up, top-down predictions play a significant role in guiding speech perception (Arnal and Giraud, 2012; Gagnepain et al., 2012; Poeppel et al., 2008) presumably across different frequency channels and processing timescales (Wang, 2010; Bastos et al., 2012; Fontolan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about speech perception supported by citations.

claim: Theta activity might be at the interface of bottom-up and top-down processes.
source: Experimental findings suggest that theta activity might be at the interface of bottom-up and top-down processes (Peelle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a suggestion based on experimental findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Theta auditory activity is better synchronized to speech modulations when speech is intelligible, irrespective of its temporal or spectral structure.
source: Theta auditory activity is better synchronized to speech modulations when speech is intelligible, irrespective of its temporal or spectral structure (Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Peelle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an empirical observation supported by citations.

claim: Theta activity bears an intrinsic temporal predictive function: it is driven by speech modulations, but is also resilient enough to syllable length variations to stay tuned to the global statistics of speech.
source: In the present model, theta activity bears an intrinsic temporal predictive function: it is driven by speech modulations, but is also resilient enough to syllable length variations to stay tuned to the global statistics of speech (average syllable duration).
evidence: This is a characterization of the model's theta activity based on the results.

claim: The model performed well above chance level when decoding syllables from a new speaker, showing flexibility in syllable tracking within a 3 to 9 Hz range.
source: The model performed well above chance level when decoding syllables from a new speaker, showing flexibility in syllable tracking within a 3 to 9 Hz range.
evidence: This is a result from the cross-speaker analysis.

claim: The model provides a direct evidence that theta/gamma coupled oscillations can be a viable instrument to de-multiplex speech.
source: In conclusion, our model provides a direct evidence that theta/gamma coupled oscillations can be a viable instrument to de-multiplex speech, and by extension to analyse complex sensory scenes at different timescales in parallel.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: By tying the gamma-organized spiking to the syllable boundaries, theta activity allows for decoding individual syllables in continuous speech streams.
source: By tying the gamma-organized spiking to the syllable boundaries, theta activity allows for decoding individual syllables in continuous speech streams.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the model's mechanism.

claim: The model demonstrates the computational value of neural oscillations for parsing sensory stimuli based on their temporal properties.
source: The model demonstrates the computational value of neural oscillations for parsing sensory stimuli based on their temporal properties and offers new perspectives for syllable-based automatic speech recognition (Wu et al., 1997) and brain-machine interfaces using oscillation-based neuromorphic algorithms.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the model, supported by a citation.
